title: What If Human Flourishing Became Part of the Measure?
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer starts from an ordinary morning in a jury assembly room, where a well-run but dehumanizing process made her ask whether the experience of the people inside a system should count toward its success. She argues that institutions have grown sophisticated at measuring revenue, productivity and test scores while the measurement has quietly become the outcome. Her proposal is to add human flourishing to the measure, asking whether people are healthier, more connected, more capable and more hopeful. She applies the same question to artificial intelligence, warning that if speed, extraction and profit are the metrics, those are the values the systems will amplify. As practical steps, a citizen leader can notice where human experience has dropped out of the measures, ask what a system is producing for the people who experience it, and value ordinary acts of care. The jury room itself changed as strangers began to talk, which she takes as evidence that the capacity for community is still alive.
points: Schafer argues that measurement has displaced the outcome: institutions track revenue, scores and efficiency without asking what the improved system does for real lives.
She proposes human flourishing as an added measure, with questions about health, connection, capability, hope and dignity.
She warns that AI built around dominance, extraction and speed will amplify those values unless a flourishing question is asked of it.
A concrete leadership move is to ask in any meeting, 'What is this producing for the people who experience it?'
Her jury-room story shows that given time together, strangers spontaneously form community, which she offers as grounds for hope.
quotes: We measure revenue, productivity, growth, utilization, efficiency, return on investment, test scores, patient volume, housing units, voter turnout, program participation, and countless other things. Many of those measures are important.
But somewhere along the way, I wonder whether we have allowed the measurement to become the outcome.
A structure can become more efficient while making life worse for the people inside it. An organization can grow while exhausting the people who make that growth possible.
We need economic measures. We need institutional measures. We also need to restore something that feels almost embarrassingly obvious: human flourishing should be part of the measure.
If dominance, extraction, competition, speed, and profit are the primary measures of success, we should not be surprised if those are the values the systems amplify.
Sometimes simply asking, “What is this producing for the people who experience it?” can change the direction of an entire conversation.
Strangers began doing what human beings tend to do when given enough time together: we began making a little community out of the circumstances we had been handed.
